title: Paris Perdikaris: When And Why PINNs Fail To Train
speaker: Paris Perdikaris
one_sentence: This lecture explains that physics-informed neural networks fail not because the idea of adding physics is wrong, but because the resulting optimization problem can become stiff, spectrally biased, and badly balanced across loss terms.
core_problem: PINNs turn a PDE problem into a composite neural-network training problem: fit data, boundary conditions, initial conditions, and PDE residuals at the same time. That sounds elegant, but the optimizer may not give each constraint useful gradient signal, especially for high-frequency, multiscale, or boundary-sensitive solutions.
first_principles_model: A PINN represents the unknown field with a differentiable neural network. Automatic differentiation evaluates derivatives, the PDE residual becomes a loss term, and gradient descent updates the network. The real object being solved is therefore not just the PDE; it is a constrained optimization dynamics. If that dynamics is stiff or biased, the PDE can be simple while training still fails.
key_claims: Physics can be inserted through architecture-level inductive bias or through loss-level regularization; PINNs mostly use the second route.
PINNs are unconventional regularizers because they regularize the function output and its derivatives rather than just the network weights.
Even simple linear elliptic problems can fail if the training dynamics cannot satisfy boundary conditions or high-frequency structure.
PINN gradient flow can become stiff, forcing impractically small learning rates if trained naively.
Different loss terms can produce imbalanced gradients, so one constraint can dominate while another receives almost no useful update.
Neural tangent kernel analysis helps diagnose spectral bias: low-frequency components are learned faster than high-frequency components.

important_terms.meaning: A neural network trained to represent a solution field while penalizing violations of a governing differential equation and its boundary or initial conditions.
A training objective made from several terms, such as data mismatch, boundary loss, initial-condition loss, and PDE residual loss.
A training pathology where the continuous-time optimization dynamics contains widely separated scales, making stable gradient descent require tiny steps.
A failure mode where different loss components produce very different gradient magnitudes, so some constraints are effectively ignored.
The tendency of standard neural networks trained by gradient descent to learn low-frequency functions before high-frequency functions.

stanford_connections: This is the natural starting point for the playlist because it separates the PINN idea from PINN trainability.
It connects to later talks on weak forms, adaptive weighting, operator learning, and structure-preserving architectures.
It gives a diagnostic mindset: do not ask only whether the physics loss is correct; ask whether the optimizer can actually use it.
practical_caution: Do not treat a small PDE residual term as proof that the learned field is physically reliable. The loss weights, collocation points, network architecture, optimizer, and frequency content can all change whether the method is solving the intended problem.
selected_evidence: Failure can happen at any time even for the simplest problems.
This gradient flow problem becomes very stiff.
Stiffness leads to imbalance gradients during back propagation.
The network cannot really change the parameters in order to fit the boundary condition.
Neural networks are known to suffer from spectral bias.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that PINNs are optimization systems, not magic PDE solvers. Their success depends on whether the training dynamics can transmit the right physical constraints into the right function components.

title: Donsub Rim: Distilling Nonlinear Shock Waves
speaker: Donsub Rim
one_sentence: This lecture explains why classical linear reduced-order models struggle on transport-dominated problems and how nonlinear representations can capture moving shocks and interfaces more efficiently.
core_problem: Classical ROMs assume a solution manifold can be well represented by a low-dimensional linear space. Transport-dominated problems break that assumption: a pulse or shock moving across a domain can generate many nearly orthogonal snapshots, so linear rank grows even when the underlying motion is simple.
first_principles_model: For transport, the low-dimensional object is often not the field values themselves but the map that moves information through space. If a feature is translated, the set of snapshots may be high-rank, while the characteristic flow or deformation map may be low-dimensional. Nonlinear model reduction tries to represent that moving geometry directly.
key_claims: Transport-dominated and moving-interface problems are hard for traditional reduced models.
Kolmogorov n-width explains why a linear basis can need many modes even for simple moving discontinuities.
The solution manifold may be high-rank while the characteristic map that transports the solution is low-dimensional.
Nonlinear reduced representations can be built by composing reduced bases with learned or constructed maps.
Shock formation creates additional difficulty because the characteristic representation can break or become non-smooth.
Deep networks can be interpreted as a way to distill a large solution representation into a smaller nonlinear reduced network.

important_terms.meaning: A PDE problem where motion, advection, shocks, or interfaces dominate the dynamics.
A measure of how well a solution manifold can be approximated by an n-dimensional linear subspace.
A map describing how points or features move through the domain under transport dynamics.
A reduced model that approximates a solution manifold using nonlinear coordinates or transformations instead of only a linear basis.
A specialized compact neural representation intended to approximate a solution family more efficiently than a large generic network.

stanford_connections: This connects directly to the reduced-order modeling concept page and gives the first major exception to linear ROM intuition.
It prepares later lectures on nonlinear manifolds, registration-based reduction, and latent-space simulation.
It also explains why data-driven simulation cannot ignore geometry: a simple translation can look high-dimensional in raw coordinates.
practical_caution: If a ROM fails on shocks or advection, the problem may not be lack of data. The coordinate system may be wrong: the low-dimensional structure may live in transport maps, not in linear combinations of snapshots.
selected_evidence: Transport dominated problems are hard to handle with traditional reduced models.
Low-dimensional reduced spaces cannot exist.
The solution manifold itself is not low rank.
There is still a low dimensional structure available.
When there's shock formation.
takeaway: The lecture's key move is to distinguish low-dimensional physics from low-rank snapshots. Moving waves can be simple in the right coordinates and expensive in the wrong ones.

title: Jan Hesthaven: Non-Intrusive ROMs Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks
speaker: Jan Hesthaven
one_sentence: This lecture frames neural networks as tools for removing bottlenecks in reduced-order modeling, especially when the full simulator is a black box and projection-based intrusive access is unavailable.
core_problem: Projection-based ROMs are powerful when you can access the governing operators, but many real solvers are legacy, classified, commercial, or otherwise black-box. For nonlinear problems, even intrusive ROMs can lose speed because evaluating projected nonlinear operators may require returning to the full state dimension.
first_principles_model: A ROM trades generality for speed by learning a compact map from parameters to solution coefficients. If the full operator is accessible, projection gives equations for those coefficients. If the operator is not accessible, a neural network can learn the parameter-to-coefficient map from simulator input-output data, and physics-informed terms can improve consistency.
key_claims: Reduced-order modeling accelerates repeated parameterized PDE solves by representing solutions in a low-dimensional basis.
Nonlinear problems introduce a bottleneck because projected nonlinear operators may still depend on the full-order state.
Non-intrusive ROMs are needed when the solver is only available as an input-output code.
A neural network can map parameters directly to reduced-basis expansion coefficients.
If a good reduced basis exists, the parameter-to-coefficient map should often be smooth enough for a small neural network.
Physics-informed neural nets can be used as part of ROM construction rather than as a wholesale replacement for numerical analysis.

important_terms.meaning: A reduced-order model that requires access to the solver operators or internal discretized equations.
A reduced-order model built from input-output data without modifying or inspecting the full solver.
The low-dimensional coordinates multiplying reduced basis vectors to reconstruct an approximate solution.
The cost or access problem that appears when reduced equations require full-order operator evaluations.
A failure mode where the neural parameter-to-coefficient map is too rich for the available simulator samples.

stanford_connections: This gives the practical ROM workflow behind many later talks: offline snapshots, reduced basis construction, online fast prediction.
It links PINNs to a narrower engineering role: solving ROM bottlenecks rather than replacing full solvers.
It connects to uncertainty and design loops because ROMs are most useful when many repeated simulations are required.
practical_caution: A neural ROM is only useful if the reduced basis is good and the learned coefficient map generalizes. Increasing neural-network size without enough simulator data can make the online predictor worse.
selected_evidence: Creating the reduced model becomes intrusive.
All you have is a piece of code that can provide you input output.
The key problem becomes how to go from choosing a parameter.
Let's use a neural net for this exercise.
When you don't have enough data... you're overfitting.
takeaway: The lecture's central lesson is pragmatic: use neural networks where classical ROM workflows have bottlenecks, especially black-box solvers and nonlinear coefficient maps.

title: Nils Thuerey: Differentiable Physics Simulations For Deep Learning
speaker: Nils Thuerey
one_sentence: This lecture argues for tightly coupling simulators and deep learning by making the simulator differentiable, so gradients from physical dynamics can guide learning, inverse problems, and control.
core_problem: Using simulators only as data generators creates a weak connection between physics and learning. Many applications need the model to know how changing an input, parameter, or control would change the simulated outcome. That requires gradients through the simulator.
first_principles_model: A simulator maps initial states, parameters, or controls to future physical states. If we can differentiate that map, we can optimize causes from effects: reduce numerical error, infer controls, improve designs, and train networks inside the physical loop. The simulator becomes part of the computational graph rather than an external data source.
key_claims: Physical models and numerical methods are valuable and should be kept where possible, while learning handles errors, observations, and uncertain components.
Forward simulation predicts what happens; inverse problems ask what inputs or controls would produce a desired outcome.
Supervised learning from simulator data is useful but loosely coupled to physics.
Putting physics only into a loss is tighter, but differentiable simulation gives a still tighter simulator-learning integration.
The key object is a gradient of the simulation with respect to the state or input.
Differentiable solvers can support solver-in-the-loop learning, control, and correction of numerical errors.

important_terms.meaning: A simulator that provides gradients of outputs with respect to inputs, states, controls, or parameters.
A learning setup where a numerical solver is part of the training loop and contributes gradient information.
A method for efficiently propagating sensitivities backward through a simulation or optimization problem.
A problem where observed or desired outcomes are used to infer hidden causes, parameters, or controls.
Learning a correction that reduces errors introduced by coarse grids, low-order methods, or approximate solvers.

stanford_connections: This is the differentiable-simulation anchor for the playlist and complements PINNs by putting the solver inside learning rather than only adding residual penalties.
It connects to control, inverse design, fluid simulation, and later foundation-model-for-science discussions.
It also gives a bridge between classical adjoint methods and modern automatic differentiation.
practical_caution: Differentiability is useful only if the gradients are meaningful and computationally feasible. Large multiphysics codes, long rollouts, discontinuities, and unstable adjoints can still make the approach hard.
selected_evidence: Ideally there shouldn't be much of a boundary between learning and simulation.
We have a gradient of this simulation.
This actually lets us combine simulation very neatly with the deep learning process.
The first example... is this solver in the loop project.
Differentiable solvers is a very useful tool.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that gradients turn simulation from a black-box data source into an optimization object. That is why differentiable physics is central to inverse problems, control, and scientific ML.

title: Pawan Goyal: Physics-Informed Learning For Nonlinear Dynamical Systems
speaker: Pawan Goyal
organization: Max Planck Institute for Dynamics of Complex Technical Systems
one_sentence: This lecture presents operator inference as a way to learn reduced dynamical models directly from data while preserving known physical structure.
core_problem: Engineering design, control, optimization, and uncertainty studies need dynamical models that can be simulated repeatedly. High-fidelity discretized models can be too expensive, and legacy or commercial codes may not expose the matrices needed for classical projection-based model reduction.
first_principles_model: A dynamical system can often be reduced to a low-dimensional state if the important behavior lies in dominant modes. Operator inference tries to learn the reduced operators directly from trajectory data, using the assumed physical structure of the governing equations so the learned model resembles the ROM that would have been obtained intrusively.
key_claims: Dynamical models are needed to analyze transient behavior under changing operating conditions.
Two bottlenecks are discretization of complex processes and the high dimensionality of high-fidelity models.
The goal is to move from PDE data directly to reduced-order models without requiring access to a discretized model.
Operator inference learns reduced operators from data while using the known structure of the physical model.
If the data are informative enough, the learned operators can approximate intrusive POD-style reduced models.
The approach is especially relevant when the data come from legacy codes, commercial solvers, or dedicated simulation toolboxes.

important_terms.meaning: A method that learns the operators of a reduced dynamical system from state trajectory data.
A detailed discretized physical model with many degrees of freedom, often too expensive for repeated simulation.
Low-dimensional directions that capture the main behavior of a high-dimensional dynamical system.
A simulator that can produce input-output data but does not easily expose internal discretization or operator matrices.
Learning constrained by known equation structure instead of fitting an unconstrained black-box predictor.

stanford_connections: This continues the non-intrusive ROM theme but focuses on learning the reduced dynamics themselves.
It connects to differentiable simulation and inverse problems because a learned reduced model can become the fast inner loop for control.
It also reinforces the series-wide pattern: use data to infer missing operators, but keep physical structure whenever possible.
practical_caution: Operator inference is not just curve fitting. If the assumed operator structure is wrong or the training trajectories do not excite important modes, the reduced model may look accurate on short rollouts and fail in prediction or control.
selected_evidence: We have focused on operator inference approach to learn dynamical systems.
We need dynamical models to analyze transient behavior.
There are two main bottleneck.
Can we go out of these two steps?
Compute reduced order model directly from the data.
takeaway: The lecture's key idea is to learn the small dynamical system that classical reduction would have produced, but to infer it directly from data when the full discretized model is unavailable or too costly.

title: Youngsoo Choi: Efficient Nonlinear Manifold Reduced Order Model
speaker: Youngsoo Choi
one_sentence: This short lecture explains how nonlinear manifold ROMs can recover accuracy on advection-dominated problems while hyper-reduction makes the nonlinear decoder practical.
core_problem: Linear-subspace ROMs are fast when solution snapshots live near a low-dimensional linear space. Advection-dominated flows, shocks, and moving structures often do not. A nonlinear manifold can represent these solution families more accurately, but naive nonlinear manifold ROMs can be slower than the full-order model because decoder and residual terms still scale with the full state dimension.
first_principles_model: A full-order simulation evolves a very large state. A ROM replaces that state with a small latent coordinate. In a linear ROM, reconstruction is a basis times coefficients. In a nonlinear manifold ROM, reconstruction is a nonlinear decoder, often learned with an autoencoder. The remaining bottleneck is that evaluating the nonlinear residual may still require full-dimensional work, so hyper-reduction samples only the terms needed to approximate the residual.
key_claims: Surrogate models are essential for multi-query settings such as design optimization because full simulations can be too expensive.
More intrusive surrogate models can be more accurate but usually require more access to the governing equations and can be harder to accelerate.
Nonlinear manifold ROMs use nonlinear maps, such as autoencoder decoders, instead of linear basis reconstruction.
Without hyper-reduction, nonlinear manifold ROMs can remain impractical because nonlinear terms still scale with the full-order model size.
Gappy POD-style sampling can reduce the number of nonlinear decoder outputs that must be computed.
On an advection-dominated viscous Burgers example, the nonlinear manifold ROM matches the full-order solution better than a linear-subspace ROM.

important_terms.meaning: A reduced-order model that reconstructs full states from latent variables using a nonlinear map rather than a linear basis.
The neural map from low-dimensional latent coordinates back to an approximate full-order state.
A technique that reduces the cost of residual or nonlinear-term evaluation by sampling a subset of entries instead of evaluating the full vector.
A reconstruction method that uses selected samples of a field to approximate the full field in a reduced basis.
A flow where transport of features dominates and often makes linear reduced spaces inefficient.

stanford_connections: This is a compact continuation of the shock-wave lecture: if transport breaks linear low-rank structure, use nonlinear coordinates.
It connects to later latent-space and autoencoder ROM talks by making the decoder cost explicit.
It also establishes a recurring DDPS theme: the representation is only half the method; the online cost model matters.
practical_caution: A nonlinear latent representation can look accurate but still be slower than the original solver if residual evaluation is not also reduced. Practical ROM design must measure both approximation error and online evaluation cost.
selected_evidence: One full simulation takes 7.4 days.
More intrusiveness means more accuracy.
NM ROM uses a non-linear manifold representation using non-linear map G.
These non-linear terms still scale with the full order model size.
NM ROM achieves less than 1% maximum relative error.
takeaway: The lecture's first-principles lesson is that nonlinear manifolds solve a representation problem, while hyper-reduction solves a cost problem. A useful ROM needs both.

title: Jesse Chan: Entropy Stable Schemes For Nonlinear Conservation Laws
speaker: Jesse Chan
one_sentence: This lecture explains entropy stability as a principled way to keep high-order discretizations of nonlinear conservation laws robust near shocks, turbulence, and under-resolved features.
core_problem: High-order numerical methods can be accurate on smooth PDE solutions but fragile on nonlinear conservation laws. Shocks, turbulence, and under-resolved gradients can cause blow-up unless the method adds filtering, limiting, or artificial viscosity. Those fixes can work, but they create a tuning tradeoff between robustness and accuracy.
first_principles_model: A nonlinear conservation law transports conserved variables through fluxes. For many physical systems there is an entropy or energy-like quantity that should satisfy an inequality. An entropy-stable discretization is built so the semi-discrete numerical scheme respects the analogous entropy inequality, making stability a structural property rather than an after-the-fact patch.
key_claims: Burgers, shallow water, Euler, Navier-Stokes, and MHD systems can be viewed through nonlinear conservation laws with entropy structure.
High-order DG methods are attractive because they combine geometric flexibility with high-order accuracy.
Under-resolved shocks and turbulence make naive high-order schemes non-robust.
Traditional stabilization through artificial viscosity, filtering, or slope limiting can reduce accuracy and require tuning.
Entropy-stable schemes use entropy variables, numerical fluxes, and discrete entropy inequalities to build robustness into the scheme.
The framework can be extended beyond collocation-style methods toward modal DG and reduced-order modeling.

important_terms.meaning: A PDE expressing that conserved quantities change through fluxes across boundaries.
A mathematical inequality for an energy-like convex entropy quantity that physically relevant solutions should satisfy.
Variables obtained by differentiating the entropy with respect to conservative variables.
A high-order finite-element-style discretization that represents solutions locally and couples cells through numerical fluxes.
Added numerical diffusion used to stabilize under-resolved features, often at the cost of accuracy.

stanford_connections: This lecture adds the numerical-analysis side of robustness to the ML-heavy talks: physical validity depends on discretization structure too.
It connects to fluid simulation and reduced-order modeling because learned or reduced models inherit stability issues from the equations they approximate.
It is a useful counterweight to black-box surrogates: before learning the solution, understand what the numerical scheme must preserve.
practical_caution: Do not evaluate a learned fluid surrogate only by short-horizon error. If the underlying conservation-law structure or entropy behavior is wrong, under-resolved shocks and turbulence can create unstable or nonphysical rollouts.
selected_evidence: They generally blow up whenever they encounter under-resolved solutions.
Shocks and turbulence... are highly under-resolved solutions most of the time.
I wanted to avoid the common metrics used for higher schemes... artificial viscosity filtering... slope limiting.
They can tend to reduce the amount of the accuracy.
A class of nonlinear conservation laws which all admit an entropy inequality.
takeaway: Entropy stability is the idea that robustness should be built from the physics of the PDE, not bolted on after the scheme starts failing.

title: Irina Tezaur: Schwarz Alternating Method For Concurrent Multiscale Coupling In Solid Mechanics
speaker: Irina Tezaur
one_sentence: This lecture presents Schwarz alternating domain decomposition as a way to couple different solid-mechanics models across scales without forcing the whole domain to use one resolution or solver.
core_problem: Engineering solids often contain localized small-scale physics that determines global behavior. Simulating the entire structure at the finest scale is too expensive, but coupling coarse and fine models can introduce artificial interface errors, incompatible solvers, and unstable information exchange.
first_principles_model: Domain decomposition splits a difficult PDE domain into subdomains. Schwarz iteration solves each subproblem while exchanging boundary or overlap information with neighboring subdomains, repeatedly updating until the coupled solution is consistent. For multiscale mechanics, this allows different discretizations, material models, or time integrators to coexist in different regions.
key_claims: Concurrent multiscale coupling is needed when a local small-scale event controls system-level performance.
The coupling method should allow different solvers and time integrators in different regions.
The interface should not introduce nonphysical artifacts.
Schwarz alternating methods decompose a complex domain into simpler subdomains and iteratively build the global solution.
The approach has convergence theory for finite-deformation quasistatic nonlinear PDEs.
Small overlap regions can be sufficient in practical examples, but non-overlapping and contact cases require additional care.

important_terms.meaning: A simulation approach where different scales are solved at the same time in different parts of the domain.
An iterative domain-decomposition method that solves subdomain problems and exchanges boundary or overlap information.
A shared region between subdomains used to pass solution information and promote convergence.
A mechanics regime where deformations are large enough that nonlinear geometry and material response matter.
A nonphysical behavior introduced by coupling models or meshes incorrectly across a subdomain boundary.

stanford_connections: This lecture broadens DDPS from learned surrogates to hybrid numerical coupling: not every data-driven physical simulation problem is solved by replacing the solver.
It connects to hybrid twins because real systems often need local high-fidelity patches inside larger coarse models.
It also reinforces the importance of interface conditions, a recurring issue in multiphysics and differentiable-simulation workflows.
practical_caution: A multiscale simulation can fail at the coupling interface even if each submodel is correct in isolation. The handoff of boundary, overlap, or contact information is part of the model.
selected_evidence: A small-scale event will eventually determine the performance of the entire system.
Allow us to use different solvers and time integrators in different regions.
We don't want the coupling to introduce any non-physical artifacts.
The earliest known domain decomposition method.
You decompose that domain into simpler subdomains.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that multiscale modeling is an interface problem: the global prediction is only as trustworthy as the exchange rule between local and coarse physics.

title: Steven Brunton: Interpretable And Generalizable Machine Learning For Fluid Mechanics
speaker: Steven Brunton
one_sentence: This lecture argues that fluid ML should prefer parsimonious, interpretable, physically meaningful models that generalize beyond the data distribution.
core_problem: Fluid mechanics produces high-dimensional data and expensive simulations, but black-box prediction alone is not enough. A model can reproduce seen trajectories while failing under new regimes, controls, geometries, or parameters if it has not captured the sparse physical structure behind the flow.
first_principles_model: Many fluid systems are high-dimensional in measurement space but lower-dimensional in the right coordinates, and their governing dynamics often use only a sparse subset of possible terms. Interpretable ML tries to discover those coordinates, active terms, closures, or discrepancy corrections rather than learning an opaque input-output map.
key_claims: Machine learning for engineering can be viewed as optimization and regression over rich data.
Generalization requires more than fitting trajectories; models should capture simple structure where it exists.
The principle of parsimony motivates sparse models: as simple as possible, but no simpler.
Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) learns governing equations from measured states and derivatives.
Choosing the right coordinate system can turn a high-dimensional fluid problem into a low-dimensional model.
ML can also focus on discrepancy modeling: learning the mismatch between an imperfect physical model and observed dynamics.

important_terms.meaning: The modeling principle that a useful explanation should use the simplest structure sufficient to describe the phenomenon.
Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics, a method that selects a small number of active terms from a library of candidate dynamics.
Regression that encourages most candidate coefficients to be zero, leaving only the important terms.
Finding variables in which complicated high-dimensional dynamics become simpler.
Learning the mismatch term between an approximate physical model and the true observed system.

stanford_connections: This is the conceptual bridge between ROMs, operator inference, and scientific ML: learn structure, not just outputs.
It connects to later surrogate and closure talks because closures are often discrepancy models for unresolved physics.
It also gives a benchmark for interpretability: can the learned object be inspected as equations, modes, balances, or correction terms?
practical_caution: A neural model that forecasts fluid snapshots may still be scientifically weak if it does not expose the variables, balances, or closure terms driving the flow. Generalization should be tested under changed regimes, not only interpolation.
selected_evidence: It would not generalize beyond fall.
Things should be as simple as possible and no simpler.
Mathematically today in my opinion is sparsity.
Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics or SINDy.
If we pull out the right coordinate system you can get a very very simple model.
takeaway: The lecture's first-principles message is that interpretability is not cosmetic. In fluids, interpretable structure is often what makes out-of-distribution generalization possible.

title: Alfio Quarteroni: The Mathematical Heart
speaker: Alfio Quarteroni
one_sentence: This lecture treats the heart as a coupled multiphysics, multiscale simulation problem spanning electrophysiology, mechanics, blood flow, valves, circulation, and coronary perfusion.
core_problem: Heart function is not a single PDE or a single simulator. Electrical activation drives contraction; contraction deforms tissue; deformation moves blood; valves open and close; coronary flow perfuses the myocardium; and the whole organ couples to external circulation. Each subsystem has different scales, meshes, equations, and numerical requirements.
first_principles_model: A computational heart model starts from geometry, meshes, and core cardiac physics modules. Electrophysiology models electrical propagation through the myocardium. Active and passive mechanics model contraction and tissue deformation. Fluid dynamics models blood in chambers and vessels. Circulation and perfusion models provide boundary and network coupling. The system-level model is the coupling of these modules.
key_claims: First-principles mathematical models can describe the electrical, mechanical, and fluid-dynamical processes of the heart.
The heart is a classical multiphysics problem with multiscale behavior in space and time.
Patient-specific geometry can come from CT, MRI, atlas models, or CAD-like solid models.
Different meshes may be needed for myocardium electrophysiology/mechanics and chamber blood flow.
Core cardiac models include electrophysiology, active mechanics, passive mechanics, fluid dynamics, valve motion, and coronary perfusion.
Large finite-element and reduced-order libraries are needed because full models are computationally heavy and uncertainty matters.

important_terms.meaning: The modeling of electrical activation and propagation through heart tissue.
Cell-level contractile mechanics that generate force in response to electrical activation.
Organ-level tissue deformation due to material elasticity and loading.
Coupling between blood flow and deforming cardiac walls or valves.
Modeling blood supply through large coronary vessels and many smaller intramyocardial vessels using different-scale descriptions.

stanford_connections: This is the playlist's clean example of a hybrid multiphysics simulator where data-driven methods must respect several coupled physical modules.
It connects to ROMs because patient-specific studies and uncertainty quantification need faster surrogates of expensive heart simulations.
It connects to differentiable simulation and inverse problems because clinical use often asks for parameter estimation from patient data.
practical_caution: A model of one cardiac subsystem can be correct but clinically misleading if the coupling is wrong. The hard part is not just solving electrophysiology, mechanics, or flow separately; it is making their time scales, boundary conditions, and feedback loops consistent.
selected_evidence: Electrical, mechanical and fluid-dynamical processes occurring in the heart.
A classical multi-physics problem featuring multi-scale solutions in space and time.
They include the electrophysiology, the active mechanics... the passive mechanics... the fluid dynamics.
We need however a second grid... for simulating the fluid dynamical processes.
You have to account for variability and uncertainty.
takeaway: The heart lecture shows what first-principles scientific ML must eventually handle: not a single learned model, but a coupled computational physiology stack.

title: Byungsoo Kim: Data-Driven Methods For Fluid Simulations In Computer Graphics
speaker: Byungsoo Kim
one_sentence: This lecture explains how graphics-oriented fluid simulation uses data-driven methods to trade some physical exactness for speed, visual quality, controllability, and artist direction.
core_problem: Computer graphics needs fluid simulations that look plausible, run fast enough for production workflows, and can be controlled by artists. Scientific accuracy is valuable, but the primary objective is often visual appearance and directability rather than strict numerical fidelity.
first_principles_model: A physics-based graphics simulator generates motion for water, smoke, splashes, or related materials. Data-driven methods can replace expensive solver pieces, enhance coarse simulation detail, operate in latent space, stylize flow fields, or optimize controls through differentiable simulation. The governing constraint is not only physics; it is the production objective of plausible, controllable visual output.
key_claims: Physics-based animation has matured, but production workflows still need efficient and controllable simulation tools.
Graphics can sometimes sacrifice exact accuracy for performance, controllability, and visual appearance.
Deep learning can accelerate particle or grid-based fluid solvers and pressure solves.
Latent-space fluid solvers use autoencoders and sequence models to integrate lower-dimensional states.
Data-driven methods can enhance visual detail through turbulence synthesis, splash augmentation, and super-resolution.
Differentiable physics gives a natural interface for optimizing controllers or initial conditions toward a target state.

important_terms.meaning: A simulation workflow that lets artists control visual outcomes while retaining physical plausibility.
Applying style-transfer ideas to fluid volumes, such as smoke motifs or colorization.
Learning to add high-resolution, temporally coherent detail to coarse fluid simulations.
A solver that evolves compressed latent representations instead of full-resolution fields.
Using gradients through a simulator to optimize motion controllers or initial states.

stanford_connections: This talk clarifies that DDPS objectives vary by domain: graphics values controllability and appearance differently from engineering verification.
It connects to differentiable physics by showing a concrete creative-control use case for simulator gradients.
It also links to latent-space ROMs and super-resolution as practical examples of learned simulation acceleration.
practical_caution: A graphics surrogate should not be judged by engineering accuracy standards alone, but the reverse is also true: a visually plausible flow model may be unacceptable for scientific prediction or safety-critical design.
selected_evidence: For visual effect artists it is necessary to have a physically plausible but computational efficient and also art-directable simulation tool.
It's allowed to sacrifice accuracy to some extent for performance and controllability.
Deep learning methods can provide faster realistic and more controllable simulations.
Latent space fluid solvers with auto encoders and LSTM architectures.
Differentiability... optimize its motion controller or initial parameter settings to achieve a target state.
takeaway: The lecture's first-principles lesson is that the evaluation target defines the simulator: graphics DDPS optimizes plausible controllable appearance, while engineering DDPS optimizes predictive reliability.

title: Karthik Duraisamy: Towards Robust, Accurate And Tractable Reduced-Order Models
speaker: Karthik Duraisamy
one_sentence: This lecture frames practical ROM development around three simultaneous requirements: robustness, accuracy, and tractability for multiscale multiphysics systems.
core_problem: Projection ROMs are attractive because they replace a huge full-order system with a lower-dimensional model, but complex flows such as combustion dynamics combine stiffness, transport, acoustics, heat release, changing topology, and nonlinear residuals. A ROM that is accurate on one condition may become unstable, inconsistent, or too expensive when the physics or parameters change.
first_principles_model: A ROM approximates the governing equations on a lower-dimensional manifold. For nonlinear systems, the reduced coordinates do not automatically make the residual cheap, stable, or conservative. Robust ROM design therefore needs structure-preserving variables and discretely consistent residual minimization for stability, adaptivity for parameter changes, and hyper-reduction for reducing residual evaluation cost.
key_claims: Reduced-order modeling means solving the same governing equations on a lower-dimensional manifold.
Complex multiphysics flows create ROM challenges through stiffness, multiscale structure, transport, and topology changes.
Basic Galerkin ROMs can be appealing theoretically but may be unstable in difficult regimes.
Least-squares Petrov-Galerkin-style formulations can improve discrete consistency and robustness.
Hyper-reduction is required because nonlinear residual evaluation can still scale with the full-order model size.
Tractability matters most when full-order simulations are so expensive that even generating training data becomes difficult.

important_terms.meaning: A reduced model that remains stable and physically consistent under challenging dynamics or parameter changes.
A projection approach that minimizes a discrete residual over a trial space rather than only enforcing a standard Galerkin condition.
A change of variables designed to preserve conservation, symmetry, conditioning, or other important mathematical properties.
Reducing online cost by evaluating nonlinear residuals or operators at selected samples instead of all full-order degrees of freedom.
A reduced model built for a subsystem that can be coupled with other reduced or full-order components.

stanford_connections: This lecture synthesizes the earlier ROM talks into an engineering checklist: accuracy alone is not enough.
It connects to hybrid twins because a deployable digital twin needs stable reduced components, not just fast surrogates.
It also links to entropy-stable schemes and differentiable simulation by emphasizing consistency between numerical structure and learned/reduced models.
practical_caution: A ROM can fail even when the basis is good if the residual is inconsistent, the nonlinear terms are not hyper-reduced, or the operating condition changes the flow topology. Always evaluate stability, cost, and parameter adaptivity together.
selected_evidence: The first part is on robustness and accuracy.
The third part of the talk is on tractability.
How to handle things like chaotic flows and big parameter changes.
For many problems stability is a major issue.
Hyper reduction... ensuring that the residual is only evaluated at a few points.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that reduced dimension is not the same as reduced difficulty. Practical ROMs must preserve structure, adapt to changing physics, and reduce nonlinear evaluation cost.

title: Mario Ohlberger: Model Reduction With Adaptive Enrichment For Large Scale PDE-Constrained Optimization
speaker: Mario Ohlberger
one_sentence: This lecture explains adaptive enrichment as a way to use reduced models inside large-scale PDE-constrained optimization without paying the full offline cost upfront.
core_problem: Classical reduced-basis workflows rely on an expensive offline stage that builds a rich reduced space before online queries become cheap. In large-scale PDE-constrained optimization, uncertainty quantification, battery degradation, and multiscale settings, the offline solves themselves can be prohibitive, and a fixed reduced space may not be accurate where the optimizer actually travels.
first_principles_model: A PDE-constrained optimization problem repeatedly solves a PDE while changing design or control variables. A reduced basis can accelerate those solves, but the optimizer must know when the reduced model is trustworthy. Adaptive enrichment starts with a smaller model and enriches it during the optimization process, often inside a trust-region framework that limits reduced-model use to regions where error is controlled.
key_claims: Adaptive enrichment goes beyond the classical offline-online splitting of reduced-basis methods.
The target setting is large-scale PDE-constrained optimization and related uncertainty quantification problems.
Classical offline construction can require very large-scale solves and become prohibitive.
Reduced-basis methods need efficient a posteriori error estimators to identify where the current basis is weak.
Trust-region ideas can control when an approximate reduced model is reliable enough for optimization steps.
For hyperbolic, shock-forming, or slow Kolmogorov-width problems, linear reduced spaces may need nonlinear extensions.

important_terms.meaning: An optimization problem whose feasible states are governed by a partial differential equation.
Growing the reduced basis during the solve or optimization process when the current reduced model is insufficient.
A low-dimensional space built from representative full-order solutions to accelerate later PDE solves.
A computable estimate of the reduced model error after a solution has been produced.
An optimization region where the approximate model is judged reliable enough to guide a step.

stanford_connections: This extends the ROM discussion from prediction to optimization loops, where repeated solves and reliability guarantees matter.
It connects to inverse problems and control because optimization requires deciding when a cheap model can replace an expensive PDE solve.
It also foreshadows nonlinear ROM talks by noting that linear reduced spaces cannot beat slow Kolmogorov-width decay.
practical_caution: Do not build a giant offline reduced basis by default. If the optimizer only visits a small portion of parameter space, adaptive enrichment can spend expensive full-order solves where they are actually needed.
selected_evidence: A new paradigm that goes beyond the classical offline online splitting.
Large scale PDE constraint optimization.
The classical approach has limitations because in the offline stage we usually need to solve very large scale problems.
Reduced basis trust region approach.
You will never beat the Kolmogorov... with a linear method.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that ROMs in optimization must be managed dynamically: use the cheap model when valid, enrich it when needed, and let error control govern the loop.

title: Tommaso Taddei: Registration-Based Model Reduction Of Parameterized Advection-Dominated PDEs
speaker: Tommaso Taddei
one_sentence: This lecture presents registration as a way to align moving features in advection-dominated PDEs so that a linear reduced model becomes effective in transformed coordinates.
core_problem: Advection-dominated problems often contain parameter-dependent moving discontinuities, fronts, or shocks. In raw coordinates, these features make the solution manifold poorly approximated by a low-dimensional linear subspace. Standard projection ROMs then need too many modes or fail to preserve sharp features.
first_principles_model: Registration introduces a mapping from the physical domain to a reference domain that aligns local solution features across parameter values. Once transported features are aligned, the transformed snapshots can become more linearly compressible. A reduced model can then combine registration, projection, and hyper-reduction to produce faster approximations.
key_claims: Parameterized advection-dominated PDEs are difficult for model reduction because moving features are not well represented by fixed linear spaces.
Registration aligns local features in a reference configuration to improve compressibility of the solution manifold.
The method is intended to be largely equation-independent, focusing on geometric alignment before reduced modeling.
Registration can be paired with projection-based and multifidelity reduced modeling.
Hyper-reduced least-squares Petrov-Galerkin ingredients are part of the proposed workflow.
The transcript ASR is poor, so the strongest evidence comes from the talk abstract and only broad transcript fragments.

important_terms.meaning: A procedure that finds transformations aligning solution features across samples or parameter values.
A common coordinate frame where transported or moving features are aligned before approximation.
A PDE where transport of features dominates the behavior and often creates moving fronts or discontinuities.
How well a family of solutions can be represented by a low-dimensional linear space.
A reduced modeling approach that combines data or models of different accuracy and cost.

stanford_connections: This is the geometric counterpart to the nonlinear manifold ROM lectures: move the data into better coordinates before reducing it.
It connects directly to shock-wave and transport-dominated discussions because moving discontinuities create high apparent rank.
It also gives a useful pattern for scientific ML: sometimes the best model improvement is a physically meaningful preprocessing map.
practical_caution: The local transcript for this talk is heavily corrupted by ASR. The deep dive should be treated as a conservative abstract-backed primer until a cleaner transcript or paper notes are added.
selected_evidence: Parameterized advection-dominated problems.
Parameter-dependent discontinuities that cannot be adequately represented through linear approximation spaces.
Registration procedure to align local features in a fixed reference domain.
Improve the linear compressibility of the solution manifold.
Registration based projection based multi fidelity model.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that transport problems may become reducible only after alignment. Registration tries to reduce motion before reducing state dimension.

title: Francisco Chinesta: Empowering Hybrid Twins From Physics-Informed Artificial Intelligence
speaker: Francisco Chinesta
organization: ENSAM Institute of Technology / ESI Group
one_sentence: This lecture describes hybrid twins as the combination of physics-based models with learned gap models that correct what the physics model misses.
core_problem: A classical simulator is only a model of reality. Industrial users increasingly care about real system performance under real loading histories, so the twin must represent both known physics and the unmodeled deviation between simulation and measurement. Pure physics may be incomplete; pure data may be unstructured and unreliable.
first_principles_model: The lecture's central equation is reality equals known physics plus ignorance. A hybrid twin keeps the physics-based model for the known part and learns a data-driven model of the gap between predictions and measurements. When the physics model and deviation model are combined, the virtual twin becomes closer to the real system and can support diagnosis and prognosis.
key_claims: Industrial modeling is shifting from selling products to guaranteeing performance under real usage.
A physics model is an approximation, so mismatch between prediction and measurement should be modeled explicitly.
Hybrid twins combine physics-based simulation with a data-driven model of the gap.
The learned gap model should respect physical consistency, including thermodynamic constraints when relevant.
Once the twin matches reality better, it can support diagnosis from data and prognosis about future behavior.
Model order reduction, regression, and machine learning can be viewed as related approximation tools in this hybrid paradigm.

important_terms.meaning: A digital twin that combines mechanistic simulation with learned correction or gap models.
The difference between what a physics model predicts and what the real system measures.
Using current observations to infer the present state or defect of a system.
Predicting future system behavior or failure based on the updated twin.
A constraint that learned material or process models should not violate basic thermodynamic laws.

stanford_connections: This is the clearest DDPS framing for hybrid physics-ML systems: learn the missing part, not the whole world from scratch.
It connects to robust ROMs because fast reduced physics models often form the core of a real-time twin.
It also connects to uncertainty and control because diagnosis and prognosis require the twin to stay aligned with real observations.
practical_caution: A digital twin is not just a dashboard or a trained surrogate. If it does not separate known physics from learned deviation, it becomes hard to know when it is extrapolating beyond its evidence.
selected_evidence: Reality... is equal to the things that you know... plus the things that you ignore.
The physics-based model... can be enriched with a data-driven model of the gap between predictions and measurements.
When you put both together... you obtain the physical reality.
Digital twin of the deviation.
Data serves in order to make diagnosis... and... prognosis.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that hybrid twins are gap models around physics: keep what you know, learn what you do not, and update the twin against reality.

title: Priya Donti: Incorporating Power System Physics Into Deep Learning Via Implicit Layers
speaker: Priya Donti
one_sentence: This lecture explains implicit layers as a way to put power-system constraints, optimization problems, and control structure inside neural networks.
core_problem: Deep learning models can be accurate statistically while violating the hard physics and operational constraints of an electric grid. Power systems require supply-demand balance, network feasibility, stability, and constraint satisfaction, so predictions are only useful if they integrate with the optimization and control problems that operators must solve.
first_principles_model: A neural network layer does not have to be an explicit formula. It can be the solution of an implicit problem: an optimization problem, differential equation, equilibrium, or control rule. If that implicit problem is differentiable through its optimality or KKT conditions, the layer can be trained end-to-end while enforcing domain structure.
key_claims: Implicit layers can encode rich functions such as optimization problems, differential equations, and other structured computations.
Power-system physics and hard constraints can be incorporated into deep networks rather than handled only after prediction.
AC optimal power flow can be embedded by differentiating through a sequence of optimization steps or through KKT conditions.
Decision-driven models can optimize for downstream system performance rather than only forecast error.
Implicit layers can provide inductive bias by reflecting the physical relationships of the domain.
They can also enforce hard constraints and support robust control in physical systems.

important_terms.meaning: A neural network layer defined by the solution of an equation, optimization problem, or dynamical system rather than by a direct feedforward formula.
An optimization problem that chooses power generation and flows while satisfying network and physical constraints.
Optimality conditions used to characterize and differentiate constrained optimization solutions.
Training a predictive model according to the quality of the downstream decision it enables.
A requirement that must be satisfied exactly or provably, not merely encouraged by a soft penalty.

stanford_connections: This talk broadens physics-informed learning from PDE residuals to optimization layers and operational constraints.
It connects to inverse problems and control because the model is trained around the decision or control problem it serves.
It also complements differentiable simulation: both make a structured physical computation part of the learning graph.
practical_caution: A low forecast error is not enough in grid applications. The learned model must be evaluated by whether it produces feasible, stable, and useful decisions under the actual power-system constraints.
selected_evidence: Incorporate physics and hard constraints from the electric power system into deep learning methods using... implicit layers.
Layers that encode... optimization problems.
Incorporate ACOPF into a neural network.
Differentiate through it... KKT conditions.
Implicit layers can be a really powerful tool for physical applications like energy systems.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that a neural model for infrastructure should include the decision physics, not just predict quantities upstream of it.

title: Traian Iliescu: Large Eddy Simulation Reduced Order Models
speaker: Traian Iliescu
one_sentence: This lecture explains LES-ROMs as reduced-order models for turbulent flows that explicitly address unresolved scales through ROM filtering and closure modeling.
core_problem: Turbulent flows contain many interacting scales. A low-dimensional ROM can represent only the largest structures, so under-resolved modes can feed back onto the resolved dynamics and destabilize or bias the prediction. Standard projection ROMs do not automatically solve this closure problem.
first_principles_model: Large eddy simulation separates resolved large scales from unresolved small scales using a filter, then models the effect of the unresolved scales through a closure term. LES-ROM applies the same idea to reduced-order models: define ROM spatial filters, evolve the resolved ROM modes, and add closure models for the effects of truncated modes.
key_claims: Reduced-order modeling for turbulence is not a settled field.
Galerkin ROMs expand the solution in data-driven basis functions and project the PDE onto that basis.
When nonlinear equations are filtered, unresolved scales create a closure term that must be modeled.
ROM closures can be functional or structural, echoing LES closure terminology.
Pressure stabilization and other practical fixes may be less elegant than theory but useful in real computations.
Scaling laws for ROM closures may be problem-specific rather than universal across all Reynolds numbers and flows.

important_terms.meaning: A turbulence simulation strategy that resolves large scales and models the effect of unresolved small scales.
A reduced-order analogue of a spatial filter that defines which scales the ROM can resolve.
The need to model the effect of unresolved or truncated scales on the resolved variables.
A functional closure idea that adds dissipative effects representing unresolved turbulent mixing.
A ROM closure approach that combines variational multiscale ideas with data-driven modeling.

stanford_connections: This connects entropy-stable fluid schemes, interpretable fluid ML, and ROMs around the common issue of unresolved scales.
It is a central caution for operator learning and neural surrogates of turbulence: the missing small scales still act on the large scales.
It also gives a first-principles reason why long-rollout validation matters for turbulent surrogate models.
practical_caution: Do not expect one ROM closure coefficient or scaling law to work across arbitrary Reynolds numbers, geometries, and flow regimes. Turbulent ROM validation must be tied to the target flow family.
selected_evidence: Reduced modeling is not... for turbulence... a settled field.
When you filter nonlinear equations you're gonna get the closure term.
The non-linear term... you have to model.
Functional means physical eddy viscosity type of thing and structural... mathematical.
Our models should not be expected to be valid over a range of Reynolds numbers.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that turbulence ROMs are filtered models. If the unresolved scales are ignored, the reduced model is not merely lower-dimensional; it is missing physics.
